item.content:encoded:
Local studio Gonzalo Bardach Architecture has created a concrete house with shading screens and green roofs for "atmospheres that support everyday inhabitation with calm and depth" in Argentina.

The screens and filtration take on a central role for the house, both conceptually and in terms of light and privacy.

"Casa JR was conceived from the idea that architecture is defined as much by what it filters as by what it reveals," Gonzalo Bardach, founder of his eponymous studio, told Dezeen.

"This project explores a calm, horizontal way of living, where concrete, light, shadow and vegetation work together to create a series of intimate spaces."

"Rather than standing as an isolated object, the house seeks to become part of its surroundings, allowing everyday life to unfold in close relation with nature and the passage of time," he continued.

The 140-square-metre house was built in San Isidro in the Buenos Aires Province and is structured as a sequence of voids and solids.

The enclosed rooms alternate with a staircase courtyard, a 30-square-metre semi-covered porch and an upper terrace that regulate the relationship between the interior and exterior without rigid hierarchies, the studio explained.

The square house is offset on the densely vegetated site.

A walkway runs from the street along the side of the house to a side entrance in the centre.

An open kitchen, dining and living room takes up most of the ground floor, spilling out onto the shaded patio through floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors.

The primary suite is on the other side of the ground floor and looks out at a rectangular pool.

Up the planted vertical circulation core, the secondary bedroom and a lounge space form an L-shaped second level that opens to a garden roof.

The house is composed entirely of sienna-toned concrete in smooth, board-formed and saw-tooth profiles that allow light and shadow to become part of the material palette with restrained timber and metal accents.

"Developed in a warm tone, close to that of earth and sunlight, [the concrete] allows for spaces where mass does not enclose, but protects, filters and creates intimacy," the studio said.

"Thick walls and filtering planes regulate views and establish a controlled relationship between inside and outside."

Read:

Studio Bright shades Melbourne home with metal screens for climbing plants

"Light enters indirectly, passing through filters, offsets and thicknesses that produce a continuous interplay between light and shadow," the team continued.

"These variations accompany the passage of the day and make time perceptible, generating atmospheres that are more experiential than formal."

The naturalistic planting strategy also filters the light, modulating views, generating shades, and creating microclimates in and around the house.

"Vegetation accompanies the architecture without dominating it, introducing seasonal variation and reinforcing the relationship with the environment," the studio said.

"The landscape does not act as a backdrop, but as an element that gradually transforms the perception of space."

The studio took a similar approach of natural integration for its Forest House in Costa Esmeralda.

Other homes recently constructed in Argentina include a Buenos Aires home enclosed in a curving concrete wall by Ademas Arquitectura, a white modular house on stilts in the mountains of Cordoba by SET Arquitectura and the renovation of a compact 1950s house also in Buenos Aires by Estudio Futuro.

School statement:

"IE School of Architecture and Design, part of IE University, brings together architecture, design, fashion and related creative disciplines across its Bachelor's and Master's programs.

"With an international outlook, the school offers a diverse educational environment that connects creative disciplines with the wider cultural, technological and business landscape.

"The school's master's portfolio spans architecture, interior design, immersive experiences, real estate development and business for architecture and design.

"Across these fields, programs combine creative thinking with practical knowledge, encouraging students to respond to evolving professional and societal challenges.

"The Master in Interior Design takes a holistic approach to spatial design, combining design development with sustainability, craft, technology, business and user experience.

"Based in Madrid, the ten-month program encourages students to consider how interiors influence wellbeing, behaviour, identity and everyday life.

"Students work through practical projects and industry-informed briefs, developing solutions that respond to real contexts and client needs.

"Across the school, IE emphasises learning by doing, interdisciplinary collaboration and engagement with professionals.

"This approach allows students to develop not only creative and technical capabilities, but also the strategic and entrepreneurial mindset needed to lead within contemporary architecture and design."

Healing the Ruin: Medicinal Planting and Hydrological Systems at the Renwick Smallpox Hospital by Nyah Nassif

"Healing the Ruin reimagines the abandoned Renwick Smallpox Hospital on Roosevelt Island as a living hydrological system, reactivating the building's original gravity-fed water infrastructure to cultivate seven medicinal and toxic plants through misting and rain-harvesting.

"Drawing on Derrida's notion of the pharmakon (substances that both heal and harm) and on hauntology, this proposal lets decay and cure coexist within the same structure rather than erasing the ruin."

Student: Nyah Nassif
Tutor: Andrea Muniáin

Territories of Care: Regenerating Lake San Pablo by Isabel Dorn

"Territories of Care confronts the looming ecological collapse of Lake San Pablo in Otavalo, Ecuador.

"Built from local bahareque and typha thatch, a family of modular structures threads along the shoreline, water-treatment plants, chinampas, drying racks, fish farms and floating algae platforms, which purify the lake while producing food, framing gastronomy and craft as tools of regeneration."

Student: Isabel Dorn
Tutor: Fernando Pino

Edible Commons: Spatial Systems for Collective Kitchens by Arianna Castro

"Edible Commons investigates the ollas comunes, the self-organised collective kitchens of Pachacamac on Lima's periphery, treating food access as a spatial rather than purely social issue.

"Its 'Scaffold Commons' is a scalable, modular system built from low-cost, reused and local materials, working across three levels (Adaptation, Co-creation, and Fabrication) to help communities improve cooking, storage and gathering conditions."

Student: Arianna Castro
Tutor: Jerónimo van Schendel

Above La Paz by Vasco Amado

"Above La Paz proposes a new typology of care on the rooftop of Hospital La Paz's oncology department in Madrid, addressing needs that clinical environments rarely meet.

"Drawing on the greenhouse as an archetype, it develops a modular timber system of four spaces (care, connection, threshold, intimacy) with a living tree nursery that uses daylight and seasonal rhythm to support patient wellbeing."

Student: Vasco Amado
Tutor: Paula Montoya

Third House: A New Music and Dance Residency & School for Migrant Minors by Lila Gaffney

"Third House transforms the Pavillon du Lac, a vacant 1863 pavilion in Marseille's Parc Borély, into a residential music and dance school for unaccompanied migrant minors awaiting minority trials and placement.

"A modular construction system inserts sleeping units, practice rooms, and performance spaces into the historic building, turning an unavoidable period of waiting into one of belonging."

Student: Lila Gaffney
Tutor: Fernando Pino

Reimagining Passive Waiting in Dubai International Airport by Aishwarya Geetharani

"This project reimagines the draining experience of waiting at Dubai International Airport Terminal 3, taking the jet bridge, the one space every passenger passes through, as its site.

"Drawing on Emirati architectural traditions, three modular configurations each cultivate a distinct state, Solitude (I), Resonance (V), and Reverie (X), using calibrated light, sound, smell and touch to give travellers more agency over how they wait."

Student: Aishwarya Geetharani
Tutor: Jerónimo van Schendel

Between Threads: How Can Fragmented Textile Practices Rebuild Community in Lucre? by Francesca Torres

"Between Threads addresses the fragmentation of textile practices in Lucre, Cusco, once home to Peru's first modern textile factory, where centralised production collapsed, but weaving endures, dispersed across households.

"Instead of introducing new activity, the project embeds a lightweight spatial system in the domestic threshold, community-built from local eucalyptus and rope, that lets homes work as connected spaces for production, learning and community life."

Student: Francesca Torres
Tutor: Paula Montoya

The Evolutionary Frequency: Suturing Soundscapes at Escudo de Veraguas Island by Ismela Marie Ruiz

"Escudo de Veraguas, a protected Panamanian island and one of the Caribbean's most biodiverse ecosystems, was closed by the government in 2024 after ecological violations, illegal construction, overfishing and noise pollution that displaced its Indigenous Ngöbe-Buglé community.

"The thesis asks how the Ngöbe-Buglé can guard the island's recovery through sound, proposing demountable tensegrity speaker structures for reefs, mangroves and forest that broadcast restorative soundscapes while combining ecological monitoring and community ritual."

Student: Ismela Marie Ruiz
Tutor: Andrea Muniáin

Life in Plastic: The Undesigned Interior by Camila Chahin

"In flood-prone Honduras, where storms like Mitch, Eta and Iota recur every few years, water is a permanent condition of domestic life rather than an accident.

"Instead of rebuilding after each flood, the project adds a flood-adaptive interior layer to the existing home, reimagining familiar furniture (beds, wardrobes, tables, refrigerators) in washable, buoyant plastic so households can adapt in place and keep the right to stay."

Student: Camila Chahin
Tutors: Andrea Muniáin

Territory Becomes Object Becomes Territory Again: The Gaucho as a Landscape Infrastructure by Carolina Estelles

"The project reimagines the gaucho as an agent of ecological repair in Argentina's Pampa Deprimida, along the Salado River.

"A nomadic, biodegradable module, built from local materials (willow branches, acacia thorns, reed fibre and cow bone) and seeded with native species, is carried on horseback and dispersed across the basin by cattle, regenerating degraded soil and wetland over decades."

Student: Carolina Estelles
Tutors: Andrea Muniáin

item.content:encoded:
Trapezoidal motifs appear throughout this concrete condominium block in Tokyo, designed by Japanese studio Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture.

Named Shin Nakano Trapezoidal, the five-storey block of 11 residential units was designed for local developer Real Partners.

According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture, the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's location on the Musashino Plateau, a large tableland in western Tokyo.

"The Musashino Plateau is one of those landscapes that people live on without ever seeing," said principal architect Ryuichi Sasaki told Dezeen.

"Our challenge was to take something as abstract as a position within a plateau and translate it into a motif that residents encounter every day," he continued.

"[It is] in the facade they walk past, in the shadows on the stairs, in the light that reaches their rooms."

On the block's eastern edge, a sheltered entrance area is framed by tall, trapezoidal concrete columns and features trapezoidal floor tiles.

A large sliding metal door leads into a lobby and stairwell, where an industrial-feeling steel staircase with grille treads allows daylight to filter through.

This lobby divides the block into three wings across which the apartments are separated, with a combination of single-storey and duplex units that extend into a basement and rooftop terrace.

Each apartment takes advantage of views over the street to the south and a park to the north, with large metal-framed windows that slide open for cross-ventilation.

The interiors are deliberately minimal and pared-back, with timber floors, exposed concrete ceilings, white-painted walls and large areas of built-in storage.

Read:

Groupwork completes "world-first" high-rise held up by stone exoskeleton

The trapezoidal motif was carried through into openings in the interior walls and floors, staircase balustrades and even the floor plan of some rooms.

Externally, the block is finished in exposed concrete, with textured trapezoidal and triangular panels created by embossing the surface of the concrete after it was poured.

"A residential building of this scale is experienced in fragments — an entrance, a stair, a window — so the motif had to work at every one of those moments," said Sasaki.

"We are proud to offer the residents of Nakano a building that connects them, quietly and daily, to the ground it stands on," he added.

Previous projects by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture include a mixed-use development containing homes and a community performance space in Tokyo, which was housed within similarly angular concrete volumes.

Elsewhere in Tokyo, Kenta Hirayama recently created the steel-clad House in Kinuta and Kenta Sano & Associates combined a glass-fronted dance studio with a house.

item.content:encoded:
This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression.

Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand outside London's Somerset House and near India House. According to Studio Saar co-founder Ananya Singhal, this location had a significant impact on the project.

"The Strand is right next to Somerset House and right next to India House," Singhal told Dezeen.

"Somerset House is where the British Navy was administered from during the colonial period, and India House is where the Indian High Commission is," he continued. "So this site has a very interesting history behind the relationship between India and the UK."

The Pangolin Shield pavilion also faces a bust of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.

To Singhal, placing the pavilion in this location was an opportunity to underline the new relationship that India has with the UK "and possibly the world", he said.

"We're an Indo-UK practice working with a British engineer, so there was something about this project and the site which kind of brought that combination together," Singhal said.

The Pangolin Shield was designed by Studio Saar and structural engineers Atelier One, led by founder Neil Thomas. It was constructed using a bamboo grid shell, which the studios wanted to use because of the material's many positive characteristics.

"It's lightweight, it's durable, it grows very quickly; once you finish with it, it's biodegradable, and you can make super interesting shapes from it," Singhal said.

The gridded shell structure that forms the base – and which is strengthened by steel fastenings – was then covered in two very different types of shields.

On top of the bamboo grid is a first layer, made from traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis, a type of bamboo stick.

This first layer is then covered by knups, woven rain shields that are traditionally used by farmers in the north-east of India.

Read:

Studio Saar creates forest-like pavilion at Design Mumbai

"The police shields were designed by the British colonial rulers to keep riots down in India all those years ago; it's really beautiful, the idea of making it a part of the structure that shelters both visitors and the locals here," Singhal said.

"The knups are from Meghalaya, the wettest place on Earth – it gets more than two metres of rain per year and its name literally means 'the land of the clouds'," he continued.

The design of the pavilion, which resembles a creature covered in scales, was also inspired by Singhal's work outside of Studio Saar.

"I'm a wildlife photographer and conservationist, and one of the animals that I hear about a lot is the pangolin, which is the most trafficked mammal on Earth," he explained. "So I wanted to create a structure that brought the pangolin into conversation."

Inside the pavilion, visitors can admire a sculpture of the pangolin and look at the drawings for the project.

As the pavilion was damaged when it was transported from India to the UK, it will be shown with an interior scaffold during London Design Festival (LDF) due to "abundant caution," Singhal said.

"It's a public space and there are going to be drunk people coming up and down this street", he said in reference to the risk of the pavilion being damaged.

Overall, Singhal believes that the project is a good representation of the values that Studio Saar stands for.

"Something which we really hold dear as a practice is the idea you can take small, humble, crafted things and combine them to make amazing things," he said.

"And that's the piece that we've practised in many areas, and what we would really love to do, and that's what we're doing here with the police shields and the knups."

Other projects on show at London Design Festival include Craft x Tech, which explores Japanese craft in a contemporary way, and Lozi's modular plywood furniture.

The photography is by Taran Wilkhu.

item.content:encoded:
Tiles decorated with hair and a dissolving washbasin made of soap are among the student projects featured in Behind Closed Doors, an exhibition by the Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents.

The exhibition featured standout projects born from a 10-week educational partnership between the bathroom brand and students of the academy's Social Design master's degree that explored the future of the bathroom.

As part of the collaboration, the students were asked to investigate how bathrooms can be reimagined in a more circular way that doesn't just conserve resources but also encourages more circular behaviours and habits in its users.

"We gave them the idea that in a circular world, Kaldewei would not produce a new bathtub anymore because we would reuse our old bathtubs, give them a new surface and build them in again," the company's head of design Christian Büttner told Dezeen.

"So what the students really explored for us was: what are the barriers against this that we have in our head?"

Among the eight featured projects, some of the most visceral explored how we can overcome the natural aversion we have against waste materials – especially ones that have passed through the hands of other people.

Design Academy students Sarah Kinzer and Moss A Moschen visited student bathrooms on their street in Eindhoven and documented the traces of use that were left behind – black mould, clumps of hair, limescale on a showerhead.

The duo abstracted these patterns in a collection of steel tiles, some even incorporating real strands of their own hair, to find beauty rather than revulsion in the intimate history of these materials.

"We try to make an aesthetic of disgust," Moschen explained. "If we want to talk about circularity, but as a society we hold expectations towards very clean and polished materials, how can we even do that?"

"So I think we just tried to flip the narrative and question what happens when something that we call disgusting is intentionally part of the design language."

In a similar vein, Carlotta Talkenberger felted a bath mat from human hair to explore the double standard inherent in using animal hair to make many of the products around us while shunning our own.

And in Ian Chu's project Wash Away Your Guilt, discarded cooking oil is turned into soap and used to form a washbasin that slowly dissolves with every use, exploring both the practical and moral implications of circularity.

"She was also questioning a little bit if circularity is a concept that we hide behind so we don't feel guilty," Moschen explained.

Read:

"Industry in Germany is no longer open to what design can do" say Currents Berlin organisers

As Europe's record-breaking heatwaves reduced the continent's water supplies to historic lows, other students shared speculative projects about how limited access to this crucial resource could reshape our habits and spaces.

A satirical film by Hanxiao Xu depicts a community that reuses its bathwater and attributes it with mythical healing properties, while Philipp Hohnerlein and Gabriela Augustyniak imagine that bathing will cease entirely.

Instead, their Bathtube project (top image) suggests tapping into the waste heat of data centres and turning their pipes into impromptu hammams, offering the warmth and comfort of a bath without the water wastage.

Nature's resources also take centre stage in a project from Guadalupe Vanini Cervini that explores the indigenous principle of the Honourable Harvest – a "covenant of reciprocity" stipulating how to responsibly take from nature and give back in return.

In this spirit, she used naturally fallen reeds from the wetlands around Eindhoven to create a series of sculptures set within that same landscape, but transported to Berlin for the sake of the exhibition.

Another exploration of more-than-human design came from Tina Lehnhardt, who created a performance around a series of costumes – embodying black mould, moisture, a dead skin cell and a humidity-loving insect known as a silverfish – to humanise the other life forms with which we share our bathrooms.

Finally, taking a more playful take on the topic, Xinliang Zhou created a simple method and instructions for how to turn everyday bathroom items into musical instruments and every shower into a jam session.

The Behind Closed Doors exhibition formed part of the inaugural Currents design festival in Berlin, which the founders argue is well on its way to establishing itself as Germany's new design capital.

Dezeen Showroom: modernist style and high levels of comfort combine in the Vipp453 Swivel chair, created by Danish brand Vipp for both conference rooms and home offices.

The Vipp453 Swivel chair is defined by its architectural silhouette, created by an aluminium frame that wraps fluidly from the arms around the padded backrest.

The backrest is substantial enough to provide comfort and support over long periods of sitting, while also giving the chair a light, airy appearance thanks to its suspended design.

Part of a line of similar chairs from Vipp, a family-owned company founded in 1939, the Vipp453 Swivel chair adds a four-star base with either castors or gliders and a 360-degree rotation.

Vipp imagines it working well in offices and conference rooms where an elevated aesthetic is desired, as well as in home offices where a bulky task chair would be unwelcome.

The chair is available upholstered in either black, camel or green leather or Dark Sand textile — finishes that continue the refined, mid-century look.

item.content:encoded:
Look-but-don't-touch design exhibitions are inherently unfulfilling so it's good that some designers are finding ways to let people properly interact with their work, writes Alice Fisher.

In the 1990s as a student in London, I got a summer job at a famous department store. I was a sales assistant for towels and robes working next to the bathroom furniture department which, true to the shop's reputation for ostentatious luxury, included some incredibly ornate toilets.

One morning, word spread around the staff that someone had – somehow – managed to use a display toilet for its intended purpose. Reactions ranged from outraged disgust to amused respect.

I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in

Personally, I was envious – imagine clambering into that sterile room set and settling on the porcelain throne. Even the most prestigious customer wouldn't get away with that.

I'm surprised how often I think about that toilet when visiting design exhibitions these days. Not for any weird reason – the only stool I like to see is one that's handmade, preferably from reclaimed wood – but because I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in.

Sadly, at most design festivals that would be as shocking and frowned upon as hopping onto the lav in a department store display.

Read:

Five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene

Looking but not touching or interacting with design is, to my mind, a strange and impotent experience. I spend so much time staring really intently at chairs trying to imagine what they feel like, when what I really want to do is loll in them.

The two things I overuse the most at London Design Festival (LDF) and other such events are my camera phone – obvs – and the surreptitious finger. You know what I mean – the index finger you slide out at hip height to feel the buttery softness of a leather chair arm, or the cool surprise of a marble tabletop, when the publicist and designer are looking the other way.

Just to be clear, I'm not stupid. I understand the financial and creative investment that studios and designers have put into these displays. I know that most of the furniture on show is a prototype or produced at great personal cost to the maker and that letting the clumsy, feckless public loose on these masterpieces is not a good idea.

Many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way

And yet… wouldn't it be great if there was an idiot-proof version of the furniture you could have a go on?

Cast your mind back over the most discussed or fondly remembered exhibits at recent design weeks and you can see I'm not the only person who feels this way. Paul Cocksedge, Alison Brooks and Waugh Thistleton all made landmark wooden LDF installations in recent years that could be sat on, walked through or even climbed up.

I'm so pleased that the AHEC exhibition Wood for the Trees, which debuted at Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design (3DD) in June, will also appear at LDF this week. The show includes beautiful rocking wooden benches by Benchmark, which are such a great place to sit.

Read:

Read LDF edition of Dezeen Dispatch online now!

Also at 3DD this year was an outsized conversation pit. This version of the 1950s favourite – in beautiful lemon linen – was a collaboration between furniture brand Vipp and Spanish architecture studio Mesura. Big enough to hold 60 people, visitors were encouraged to slip off their shoes and climb inside using swimming pool-style ladders. Most design critics opted to bounce like toddlers at soft play rather than hold a meaningful conversation, which made the experience even more delightful.

Metamorphosis in Motion by architect Lina Ghotmeh at this year's Milan design week gave a similar thrill. Watching people explore Ghotmeh's magenta maze, which filled the courtyard at the Palazzo Litta, was a pleasure.

The trend for staging shows in apartments rather than sterile showrooms also reflects how many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way. While design shop Artemest is probably the OG brand for turning fabulous apartments into even-more-fabulous fantasy exhibition spaces during Milan, I think French vintage dealer Antoine Billore's Loreto apartment for perfume house L'Artisan Parfumeur this year was the one in which I really wanted to sit down and pretend it was mine.

"I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."

British designer Charlotte Taylor's breakout show was Home from Home at 3DD 2025 (pictured). She not only curated this exhibition of work by 40 furniture designers held in an apartment at Noura Residency on Sankt Peders Stræde, but also lived in the space during the design festival.

Recently, Taylor told me that, although the idea was to get away from the "untouchable tableau" of the typical design show, she hadn't expected visitors to get quite so comfortable, quite so quickly in her personal space. "It became a performative piece, to the extent that I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."

She should have held a lottery that gave visitors the opportunity to apply to spend the night there themselves. I can think of few things that design fans would like more.

All I would like designers to do is think of any way it's possible for visitors to engage with their beautiful creations beyond the look-but-don't-touch of a standard design fair. Using a toilet absolutely crosses the line, but is sitting down, or even touching, really asking too much?

Alice Fisher is a lifestyle journalist based in London. She was previously lifestyle editor at The Observer, and has also written for The Guardian and the Financial Times, among others.

item.content:encoded:
With London Design Festival underway, we asked long-standing mayor of London Sadiq Khan for his thoughts on the festival and what to see this year.

Amy Peacock: Why do you believe London's design scene is worth investing in, and what role does London Design Festival play in this?

Sadiq Khan: London has a remarkable history of producing designs that have become global icons. Visionaries such as Thomas Heatherwick and Norman Foster have reimagined architecture and public spaces, while Vivienne Westwood revolutionised fashion with her rebellious designs, and celebrated product designer Tom Dixon and multidisciplinary artist Es Devlin are all showing why London's design is an international success story.

I'm delighted that LDF plays a key role in the success of the industry, showcasing, celebrating and developing our leading talent. The festival is an incredible advert, drawing international attention, investment and visitors as it welcomes more than 600,000 visitors.

I'm hugely proud to support the festival and over the past 10 years have invested £2.2 million that has helped to unlock £1.23 billion for the economy through jobs and investment.

Amy Peacock: What are you looking forward to seeing this year at LDF?

Sadiq Khan: London Design Festival is a huge highlight in the capital's cultural calendar because there are so many great events taking place. There's a lot to look forward to, including The Pangolin Shield, which will be a significant installation on the Strand.

There are design districts that showcase 11 neighbourhoods across the city as local studios, showrooms, galleries and cultural venues open their doors with exhibitions, installations, events and talks, while the V&A continues its long-standing relationship with the festival with Awakenings.

Amy Peacock: How does London's design scene compare to other cities? Do you think it's possible for LDF to have an impact on the scale of design festivals in Milan and Copenhagen, and how does the UK no longer being in the EU have an impact on this?

Sadiq Khan: Our capital is a powerhouse for the creative industries and LDF is a fantastic example of our influence in the design industry. The festival promotes our city's creativity, drawing in the country's greatest thinkers, practitioners, retailers and educators to deliver an unmissable celebration of design. That's why it is one of the world's leading design events and has served as the blueprint for design weeks and festivals globally.

However, there is no doubt that the UK's departure from the EU has made it harder for London's design industry to trade, collaborate and recruit talent across Europe. Increased paperwork, barriers for the movement of creative talent and reduced access to EU funding have brought challenges, but despite all this, London continues to be a thriving and welcoming place for designers.

item.content:encoded:
Designers Bahbak Hashemi-Nezhad and Rafael El Baz have used traditional biscuit moulds to create Sweet Terrain, a collection of wall tiles for a HS2 station made from clay excavated during its construction.

Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz salvaged 12 tonnes of clay dug up from the site of Old Oak Common, a station under construction in London designed by WilkinsonEyre for the high-speed rail network HS2, to make the playful collection.

The tiles have distinctive reliefs made with moulds modelled on wooden tools traditionally used to create Ma'amoul – cookies originating in the Arab world. The design draws on the designers' visits to patisseries in west London belonging to Middle Eastern bakers who migrated from Lebanon and Syria.

It is hoped to shine a light on their stories and help bring place-based identity and connections to local communities into the vast and controversial HS2 project.

"The goals were to make hyper-local objects that resonate with those who would ultimately see and use them, and in doing so instil a sense of pride and embed narrative that isn't possible with off-the-shelf products," Hashemi-Nezhad told Dezeen.

"Beyond the resourcefulness and circularity of the project, we wanted to create something meaningful, literally from the bottom up, by engaging local communities and embedding the work for the generations that follow them," added El Baz.

"Infrastructure projects, however large or small, can be humanised and made culturally resonant through design."

According to the designers, the Sweet Terrain tiles are set to be used in the station's "quiet spaces", such as multi-faith zones, toilets and corridors.

The exact number of tiles that will be used is yet to be confirmed, but Hashemi-Nezhad said the number will be in the thousands.

Sweet Terrain's initial design process began by diverting 12 tonnes of construction soil from landfill. It was then smoothed and refined, forming the ideal consistency for tile making.

Production was carried out with Craven Dunnill Jackfield – one of Britain's oldest and last remaining traditional tilemakers, which has previously created tiles for London Underground.

Read:

London Underground waste repurposed into tiles for tube stations

Together with Craven Dunnill Jackfield, the duo developed 3D scans of the biscuit moulds to form the tiles, which have been made in various sizes and depths to ensure optimal style for installation in the public realm.

"Too shallow and it loses its tactility; too proud and it risks chipping and damage due to vandalism," said Hashemi-Nezhad.

Now the designers are working with the manufacturer's glaze lab to experiment with different colour and texture finishes.

However, they are set on using hand-dipped glazes, which they believe will help add a "human touch" to the wider infrastructure project.

The bakers with whom Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz have consulted on the project have described the work as "an act of recognition".

"When these tiles enter the public realm in the new station, it will bring so much joy and pride to us bakers, as well as our communities and families," baker Vasken Jermakian of Sweetland Bakery said.

The HS2 network has been highly controversial, for reasons including its environmental impact on the Chilterns – an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) through which it cuts.

Dezeen recently published construction photos of Old Oak Common station, for which the tiles are being made. Once complete, it will be one of the largest transport interchanges in the UK.

Designer Hashemi-Nezhad is currently a designer in residence at CCA Tashkent, which recently opened its hub within a "basilica-like" tram depot overhauled by Studio KO in the Uzbekistan capital.

item.content:encoded:
White lime-rendered walls frame Casa Amona, a two-storey home and studio in Mexico, designed by local architecture studio Colar to support multi-generational living.

Perched beside a wooded hillside in San Cristóbal de las Casas, the 155-square-metre residence contains a one-bedroom house that can be adapted into a two-bed, alongside a studio and a guest bedroom.

Colar designed its angular form to prioritise views of the surrounding hillside in several directions, allowing each room to forge "a different relationship to the landscape".

This is enabled by a series of sheltered terraces that punctuate the home's upper floor, along with a combination of slim and large windows that characterise the home's exterior.

"The house is conceived as a continuous dialogue between domestic life and the landscape, with the garden becoming an active part of the spatial experience," Colar told Dezeen.

"Rather than relying on a single dominant view, the project uses different openings, orientations, and types of windows to create a series of distinct relationships with the garden and the surrounding landscape."

At the home's front, a sheltered entryway provides access to the main dwelling, while a separate entrance leads into the studio space, which sits beneath a wooden roof and is flanked by a spacious planted courtyard.

Inside, the home features a stacked layout of rooms designed to function as independent units. This includes living spaces on the ground floor and a bedroom above.

To accommodate multi-generational living, an enclosed ground-floor living space can be converted into a bedroom without architectural intervention.

Upstairs, the main bedroom space is accompanied by a small study and complemented by three terraces overlooking the landscape.

Read:

Colar revives adobe structure to create pared-back home in Mexico

"The house is organised as a series of spatially autonomous but interconnected units, allowing different forms of occupation over time," the studio said.

"The adjacent workshop, with its independent access, provides a space for artistic work and family gatherings while also allowing for autonomous living when needed."

Informed by local building techniques, the home's lime-rendered concrete blockwork and brick walls are left exposed across the interior and exterior, paired with carpentry and clay tile floors.

"The material palette draws from local building traditions while allowing their constructional logic to be expressed in a contemporary way," the studio explained.

Also in Mexico, the studio recently updated and extended a dilapidated adobe structure to create a single-storey home in Chiapas, and Studio Font perched a cliffside home in Mazunte atop a series of inhabitable concrete columns.

item.content:encoded:
Swedish studio Johan Sundberg Arkitektur has designed the Pine House holiday home with a cross-shaped plan that stretches into its forested site in southern Sweden.

Perched on a north-facing slope on the Hallandsåsen ridge, the 152-square-metre home was completed by Johan Sundberg Arkitektur in close collaboration with the clients.

It contains a three-bedroom summer house within its low-lying timber structure, designed in response to the "rhythms of daily life and the character of the landscape", the studio said.

"We wanted to make a house that connects you to the place and to how the building is made," studio founder Johan Sundberg told Dezeen.

"The cross-shaped plan reaches into different parts of the landscape, giving you both close views into the vegetation and longer views out towards the sea," he continued.

"[The clients] also wanted three equally sized bedrooms, which says something about the informal way the family wanted to use the house."

The cabin is built from a structure of cross-laminated timber (CLT) wrapped in pine panelling, left exposed and untreated to weather over time.

Wide decking wraps around the volume, creating an external walkway that is sheltered by its overhanging roof. At the home's northern end, this decking is raised on a concrete plinth, where a large window and outdoor dining terrace overlook the landscape.

"Outside, the vertical heartwood pine cladding is untreated, allowing exposure to sun and rain to gradually give different parts of the house different tones," Sundberg said.

"The eaves create a sheltered edge around the house," he continued. "You feel the protection of the roof while remaining very close to the landscape."

Read:

Kuba Woźniczka nestles black-timber holiday cabins in Polish woodland

Pine House opens into an open-plan kitchen and dining area, which is divided from a living room by a central passageway crowned by a long, deep skylight. From here, the main bedroom is accessed through a glazed studio space, joined by a bathroom and sauna.

Two additional bedrooms are held at the home's opposite end. Each bedroom has direct access to the outdoor decking, with the main bedroom opening to an outdoor shower tucked beneath the roof's overhang.

A palette of exposed materials and handmade details established by the studio alongside the clients is used throughout the interior.

In the living areas, concrete flooring is paired with wooden cabinetry, while lava-stone tiles finished in a pale green cloak the bathrooms.

"We established a basic palette of exposed spruce, concrete floors and finer Oregon pine joinery, then worked together to give the contributions from their friends and collaborators a considered place within it," Sundberg explained.

Other holiday homes recently featured on Dezeen include a charred cedar home with an "angled, folded form" in Yatsugatake by Keiji Ashizawa and a black-timber cabin nestled in a Polish woodland by Kuba Woźniczka.

The photography is by Markus Linderoth.

item.content:encoded:
From bars and hotels to private homes, this lookbook explores interiors where billiard tables are on hand for spontaneous games.

Billiard tables – comprising a cloth-covered surface surrounded by cushioned sides that are punctuated with netted pockets – are a type of table that cue sports can be played on, such as pool and snooker.

While they are traditionally covered in dark green cloth, to recall the appearance of grass lawns, contemporary designs feature differently-coloured cloth, from blues and reds to neutrals.

Brightly coloured balls make the tables instantly recognisable, standing out against the background cloth when contained in a triangular rack or strewn around the table mid-play.

The following interiors all feature billiard tables, from traditional games rooms in hospitality venues to unconventional placements in residential kitchens and living rooms.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring wooden staircases, picture windows and cottage living rooms.

Soho House São Paulo, Brazil, by Soho House

Sculptural legs, deep netted pockets and a navy top allow this monolithic billiard table to anchor a lofty games room in members' club Soho House's São Paulo outpost.

Its ornately inlayed base ties it in with pattern found elsewhere in the room, from wall hangings to lounge chairs.

Find out more about Soho House São Paulo ›

House Kala, Indonesia, by Caceres + Tous

When the panoramic jungle and sea views have been taken in, residents of this home on the Indonesian island of Lombok can retreat indoors for a game of pool.

Within a black-painted room, a billiard table with a honey-coloured wooden base and a pale, sandy-coloured tabletop allows the multicoloured balls to stand out.

Find out more about House Kala ›

Watson House Annexe, UK, by Ström Architects

A billiard table covered in sky blue cloth sits in the centre of this wood-lined bar and games room within a timber-clad annex, designed by British studio Ström Architects.

The firm designed the annex to have the atmosphere of a "rustic boutique hotel", facilitating drinking, dancing and partying in addition to extra accommodation for overnight guests.

Find out more about Watson House Annexe ›

The Bell, USA, by Ste Marie

The glamorous atmosphere of mid-century offices has been reinstated during the renovation of this 1960s tower in Chicago, including chic games rooms, a library and lounges.

A billiard table upholstered in a fawn-coloured cloth sits within one such games room, recalling a time during which "business and leisure once overlapped".

Find out more about The Bell ›

Mawi Garage, Indonesia, by Dhaniē & Sal

A fleet of cars and motorbikes are housed within this renovated garage by local architecture practice Dhaniē & Sal, who added a similarly sleek apartment and office space to the building.

Inside the apartment, a futuristic pool table with metal edges and feet, softened by a dusky rose-grey cloth top, sits in the living room.

Find out more about Mawi Garage ›

New Orleans renovation, USA, by Office La

A billiard table with a wine-red top sits where a conventional dining table would in this residential kitchen of a pink-painted house in New Orleans.

Elegant legs, leather pockets and the colourful pool balls add to the visually stimulating interior, which compiles a mosaic tiles floor, deep green cabinets, pink walls and framed artworks.

Find out more about New Orleans renovation ›

Jac's on Bond, USA, by Gachot Studios

Local design studio Gachot Studios put a billiard table with a custom-designed camel-coloured top in the back of this snug New York neighbourhood bar.

Its silvery metal-capped corners and black base ties in with the rest of the pared-back interior, populated with low mood lighting, contemporary art and black dining chairs.

Find out more about Jac's on Bond ›

item.content:encoded:
A zigzagging red facade and rooftop running track are among the key features of Jihlava Municipal Arena, completed by architecture studio Chybík + Krištof in the Czech Republic.

Located in the heart of Jihlava, the 5,650-seat building was designed for a local ice hockey team, but will also serve as a "cultural and civic hub" for the city.

It is distinguished by its bright red aluminium facade, which Chybík + Krištof designed to ensure a strong civic identity. 

According to the studio, the red nods to both the municipality's heraldry and the hockey team's club colours, while the zigzags have been compared to the spines of a hedgehog – a symbol of the city.

"We conceived the arena as a building that should feel approachable and welcoming while also meeting the complex technical demands of a large venue," said Chybík + Krištof founding partner Ondrej Chybik.

"The angular facade and its crown-like top give the arena a strong identity, connecting it to the city's historic skyline while expressing a contemporary character."

"Thanks to the red facade evoking a hedgehog as a symbol of the city, Jihlavans have strongly connected with the arena," added city councillor David Beke.

Chybík + Krištof won a competition to design Jihlava Municipal Arena, held by the local authority to replace an old ice rink. The competition asked for a venue that was better integrated with the city centre.

It is designed to host everything from concerts to conferences, in addition to ice hockey and other sports. To allow this, its design is adaptable, with retractable stands enabling the capacity to expand from 5,650 spectators for hockey to over 7,400.

"The Jihlava Municipal Arena was conceived as a public building first and an event venue second," explained Chybik.

"Positioned at the edge of Jihlava's historic centre, it is not treated as a standalone object but as an extension of the city itself," he continued.

"Through openness, permeability, and careful attention to detail at every scale, the arena supports everyday use, shared urban life, and moments of collective celebration."

Jihlava Municipal Arena's stands are made with red-pigmented concrete, combined with steel roof trusses.

On its roof is a 230-metre rooftop running track, which is free for the public to use. It also functions as a city viewpoint.

Outside the arena, public spaces were designed to help people move seamlessly between nearby buildings. This includes an arcade formed by an overhanging roof section and an amphitheatre-like staircase.

Inside, a circulation space, which is fully accessible to wheelchair users, wraps around the seating area.

"Our aim was to create a building that lives with the city every day – beyond games or concerts," said Chybik. "The arena is part of the city's structure, not an isolated island."

Read:

David Chipperfield Architects and Arup reveal Olympic ice rink in Milan

Finishing touches to the building include custom-made folding seats designed with Czech seating manufacturer Kovostal, engineered to double as acoustic treatment.

There are also triangular light fixtures embedded in the concrete structure, created by the Czech glassworks Bomma, and five light installations made by Tech-fabrika, all to designs by Chybík + Krištof.

Wayfinding is supported by visuals and a unique typeface developed by graphic designer Lukáš Kijonka as a nod to the zigzagging facade.

Alongside the stadium, the project includes a trio of auxiliary buildings. These function as a training hall and homes for operational and technical facilities.

Two of them involved repurposing existing structures on the site, while the third is a newly built structure by Chybík + Krištof that takes the form of a six-storey silver cube. This contains a fan shop, a restaurant, a hotel, a gym, and a sports hall.

Chybík + Krištof was founded in 2010 by architects Chybik and Michal Kristof. Its other recent projects include proposals for a preschool in northern India and a red-concrete tower in Tirana.

Another high-profile ice hockey arena recently completed on Dezeen include the Milano Santagiulia Ice Hockey Arena, designed by David Chipperfield Architects for the 2026 Winter Olympics.

The photography is by Laurian Ghinitoiu unless stated otherwise.

item.content:encoded:
Indents and slices across an offset gabled volume bring natural light into this beach house in Queens, New York, by Brooklyn-based BAAO Studio.

The 2,655-square-foot (247-square-metre) residence is located within a beachfront co-op in Breezy Point – a neighbourhood at the western end of the Rockaway Peninsula, which juts out into New York's Lower Bay.

The client, who grew up in the area and already owned the site, asked BAAO Studio to create a holiday home for their family of four. During the construction process the client decided to make it their permanent residence.

"They wanted an open, modern, light-flooded interior and surrounding exterior areas with dramatic spatial qualities for family life and entertaining that worked within the flood and co-op constraints on the project," said BAAO.

The area was badly impacted by Hurricane Sandy in 2012 and now has strict building codes for flood and weather protection.

The house is therefore elevated above the ground and accessed via a short flight of steps or a ramp along one side.

"FSC-certified accoya wood siding and decking from Delta Millworks was selected for the exterior for its high durability rating in marine environments," BAAO said.

An offset gabled roof tops the structure and is exposed throughout the interior spaces, including an almost triple-height great room accessed directly from the exterior.

This large, airy space is naturally lit by windows up the sides of the front-facing gabled facade, which reach all the way to the roof.

In between the glass, a central chimney stack is clad in warm oak to contrasts the white batten and board siding that wraps the remainder of the room.

Read:

BFDO completes wooden Surfboard House near Rockaway Beach

A secondary volume inside creates an upper storey towards the back, so it overlooks the main sitting area.

"The second-floor spaces are nested within the building envelope, creating the sense of a 'house within a house', with an oak-clad facade and interior windows opening into an upstairs family room," said the studio.

Beneath is a custom Henrybuilt kitchen and dining area that extend the full width of the house, in which pale stone forms a long island and backsplashes that support open shelving.

These spaces open to an outdoor deck, denoted along the exterior facade by wood that was blackened with the shou sugi ban technique.

The same treatment is applied to the planks that forms a headboard and a dividing wall in the primary bedroom, which faces a wall of windows and skylights for optimum views from the bed.

More skylights bring additional light into the other upper-level bedrooms, which are all neutrally decorated and continue the oak accents from downstairs.

BAAO was founded by Alexandra Barker in 2006, and the Brooklyn studio has worked extensively in the New York borough and beyond.

Previous projects include a daycare centre featuring curved apertures and blue tones, and another with house-shaped openings and cheerful hues, plus a townhouse extended around a magnolia tree.

The photography is courtesy of BAAO.

item.content:encoded:
Visitors to this woodland cabin in East Sussex enter via a planted roof terrace, which its architect, British studio Built Works, has "devoted entirely to the ritual of bathing".

Nestled in woodland in East Sussex, the blocky Bather's Cabin is sheathed in layers of blackened larch and topped by a lush rooftop fitted with a sauna, hot tub and ice bath.

"We wanted the rooftop deck to be devoted entirely to the ritual of bathing," Built Works told Dezeen.

"The terrace was designed to feel rooted in the woodland while also being slightly transportive and otherworldly," it continued. "A raised boardwalk floats above this roof garden, allowing guests to move through the planting and become completely immersed in the bathing ritual."

The cabin sits alongside a group of other wooden structures designed by Built Works for Architects Holiday, its hospitality company at Great Park Farm.

Among them is the aptly named Yogi's Cabin, which is built around a yoga studio, and the Drying Shed Sauna.

Bather's Cabin sits at the foot of a steep bank adjacent to a small stream on the farm, meaning guests arrive at its roof level before descending inside.

"We chose this position so that the roof terrace would sit broadly level with the top of the bank, creating an interesting interplay between the building and the site's changing levels," said the studio.

Its rooftop is coloured with mosses, grasses and ferns relocated directly from the plot on which the cabin was built, creating the feeling that "the woodland floor had been lifted into place".

The blocky form is designed to have a protective feel and is modelled on 1960s granaries on the site and others nearby. Its tiered facade was crafted from larch sourced from a local sawmill and blackened with pine tar.

"The tiered facade draws on the stepped forms of traditional granaries and grain stores," Built Works said.

"Its profile also helps to soften the cabin's silhouette within the landscape," it continued. "Although the building has a strong, almost monolithic presence, the stepped form makes its outline less precise, allowing it to merge gradually with the surrounding woodland, particularly at night."

Read:

Built Works creates Drying Shed sauna in East Sussex woodland

Inside, the plan is arranged in a cross that frames views to north, south, east and west, and organises various functions around an open central point.

According to Built Works, doors are kept to a minimum to ensure the cabin is as open as possible. Instead, curtains "provide soft divisions where privacy is needed".

Throughout the cabin, natural, locally sourced and minimally processed materials have been prioritised, with many elements also made by hand.

This includes bathroom tiles made by Built Works co-director Harry Kay with his family, featuring imprints of flowers and the fingerprints of his children.

The curtains were also handmade, block-printed with the shape of the cabin's floor plan, while the furniture was crafted from blocks of cedar to echo the building's geometric form.

Finishing touches include an inlaid, woodblock floor, hand-cut on site from English oak. UK-grown and processed hemp was used as insulation.

Built Works was founded in 2018 by Kay with Will Gowland. Its other projects include a London chocolate shop with a "peculiarly British" interior.

Other cabins recently featured on Dezeen include a holiday home by Unknown Works, which was sunk into a dune on the island of Terschelling, and a pair of Corten "tents" in New South Wales by Casey Brown Architecture.

item.content:encoded:
As Dyson seeks to disrupt the toothbrush market with its CameraJet, we look back at how the technology company has fared in its attempts to transform other product categories over the years.

Founded in Britain but now controversially headquartered in Singapore, Dyson is one of the world's most innovative companies.

Its mission-statement is to identify product categories overdue for a shake-up and leverage its extensive engineering and design capabilities to deliver something that works better for consumers.

The firm has had a string of enormous successes, as well as projects that have crashed and burned. Company founder James Dyson often casts failure as an occupational hazard of innovation, and a valuable source of learning.

Dyson's latest product – a toothbrush that flosses your teeth with mouthwash while you brush – has been met with some scepticism. Much of the criticism comes down to its hefty price tag, though the company has an undeniable track record of making high-end everyday appliances mainstream.

So, while we wait to see if Dyson can do it again with the CameraJet, here are four product types the company has previously revolutionised, as well as four it hasn't.

Four it did:

Vacuum cleaners

The story of James Dyson's invention of the bagless vacuum cleaner in 1978 is well-known.

His cyclone-based design was first licensed by the Japanese company Apex in 1986 and after some success, Dyson was able to start manufacturing through his own company in the UK.

The DC01 (pictured) launched in 1993, and looked completely different to anything else on the market. Despite the high price-point it became a runaway bestseller, and bagless vacuums are now the norm.

Dyson has continued to innovate in the years since across nearly 100 vacuum models, notably with cordless technology and a ball system for steering.

Its most recent release in the category is the PencilVac, which the company claims is the world's slimmest vacuum cleaner.

Hand dryers

Until around the turn of the millennium, the only hand dryers available in public bathrooms left a lot to be desired.

In theory, they worked by blowing warm air onto the user's hands to evaporate moisture. In practice, they seemed to do barely any drying at all, and were highly unreliable – often blasting at scorching temperatures or failing to operate entirely.

The Dyson Airblade, released in 2006, used a different system. Powered by a compact digital motor, it fired a sheet of filtered cool air at more than 400 miles per hour over hands inserted into its maw, gently stripping water off the skin.

It was not the first high-speed hand dryer – Mitsubishi's Jet Towel had become common in Japan during the 1990s, for example – but the Dyson's futuristic design and clever marketing helped it and subsequent versions to become a common fixture in restrooms across the world.

Not everyone is a fan, however. Design critic Mark Lamster even declared the Airblade "the most abhorrent work of design in recent memory".

And, as detailed in a Guardian long-read in 2019, the paper towel industry has backed a series of studies claiming that jet hand dryers like the Airblade spread more germs, which Dyson contests.

Fans

Having tackled vacuum cleaners and hand dryers, Dyson turned its attention to electric fans. It decided that the spinning blades on conventional fans – technology that dates back to 1880 – produce an unsatisfactorily uneven airflow, are tricky to clean, and dangerous to fingers.

In response, in 2009 the company unveiled the Air Multiplier, which it declared the world's first bladeless fan. With a cylindrical base containing a motor and a ring perched on top, it used a similar system to the Airblade to smoothly blow 405 litres of air per second.

Subsequent models have incorporated heating, cooling, humidifying and purifying capabilities and are a significant part of Dyson's product lineup – but have not had the same industry-wide impact as some of its other innovations, with bladed fans still a more common choice for consumers.

Hair care

With the launch of its Supersonic hair dryer in 2016, Dyson triggered a transformation of the hair-care industry.

Like the DC01, the Airblade and the Air Multiplier, the Supersonic looked markedly different to other products in its category, with a large hole in the middle.

The Supersonic is significantly lighter, quieter, quicker and gentler on hair than conventional dryers, thanks to a series of innovations developed over four years with £100 million of investment. The process even involved sending engineers to beauty school to learn how to blow-dry like professionals.

As with other Dyson products, the Supersonic was much more expensive than many competitors, but that didn't stop it from becoming the best-selling hair dryer in the UK within a month of launching.

Dyson has since followed up with multiple other hair-styling tools, while other brands have raced to develop high-performance products marketed as beneficial for hair and scalp health.

In 2020, British Vogue called the Supersonic "an industry game-changer that has sent a shockwave through the hair industry".

Read:

Our thoughts on the Dyson CameraJet toothbrush

Four it didn't:

Washing machines

Dyson's first failure came in the early 2000s. After its engineers discovered that a two-hour cycle in a conventional washing machine removed less dirt than 15 minutes of hand-washing, they set about developing a new kind of mechanism.

Released in 2000, the CR01 Contrarotator used two counter-rotating drums designed to replicate hand-washing, and was followed by a second model in 2004.

Dyson maintains that its washing machines were more energy efficient than competitors and capable of dealing with bigger loads, but in 2005 the line was discontinued due to high manufacturing costs, which meant they were selling at a loss. Dyson himself would later tell Bloomberg he should have set a higher price point for the product.

Headphones

Towards the back end of the Covid pandemic, Dyson unveiled a product that was met with widespread bemusement.

The Dyson Zone combined a set of noise-cancelling headphones with a detachable air-filtering visor. The company said its first wearable product had been six years in the making, but in the context of the global health crisis, the marketing images of people wearing the device on the London Underground carried unhappy connotations.

Dyson withdrew the Zone from sale in mid-2025, with Dyson chief engineer Jake Dyson (James's son) telling Wired the product was "completely ahead of its time".

"We have sold thousands," he said. "And we still have the tooling – but we've stopped manufacturing it. We haven't thrown the tools away. It's something we believe will come around in the future. It's a brilliant product."

The company hasn't abandoned the headphones category entirely, releasing the much more conventional OnTrac in 2024. The product received favourable reviews and has reportedly had some commercial success, although it hasn't triggered a significant shift in a crowded market.

Ventilators

Dyson had another disappointing episode early in the pandemic, though in very different circumstances.

As the coronavirus spread across Europe in March 2020, demand for ventilators exploded, leading to widespread shortages of the mechanical breathing aids.

Over just 30 days, Dyson worked with medical device company The Technology Partnership to develop the CoVent ventilator, having been called on to help bolster supplies by then-UK prime minister Boris Johnson.

The design utilised Dyson's proprietary digital motor and air-filtration technology, and was portable and easy to mount on a patient's bed. It was also designed to be simple to manufacture at volume, with plans to produce 15,000 units including 10,000 for the UK's National Health Service.

However, in late April the government told Dyson its ventilators were no longer required amid a realisation that the country's need was less than previously estimated. James Dyson said at the time that the company "don't regret our contribution to the national effort for one moment".

At the public inquiry into the UK Government's handling of the Covid pandemic, former minister Michael Gove said that the CoVent failed to pass regulatory tests.

Electric cars

In 2017, Dyson announced that it was developing an electric car. But two years and £500 million later, the project was ultimately scrapped before the first prototype could be road-tested.

"The Dyson automotive team has developed a fantastic electric car, but unfortunately it is not commercially viable," the company said at the time.

Details of the N526, as it was called, were later revealed to the Times. The car was a sporty-looking seven-seater SUV with an aluminium body, huge wheels and a sharply raking windscreen. Dashboard information would have been projected like a hologram in front of the driver, while the seats were reminiscent of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's MR Chaise.

Each car would have had to sell for £150,000 to break even, James Dyson told the paper. He said it would have been impossible to compete with other electric cars, claiming that car companies were selling electric vehicles at a loss subsidised by combustion-engine models.

"There's huge sadness and disappointment," he said. "Ours is a life of risk and of failure. We try things and they fail. Life isn't easy."

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: an exhibition during this year's Maison&Objet furniture fair in Paris is set to demonstrate the continued relevance of Hanji, a thousand-year-old Korean papermaking technique.

Located within the Paris-Nord Villepinte exhibition centre, the exhibition aims to demonstrate contemporary potential uses for Hanji, Korea's traditional handmade paper.

Hanji is primarily made from the inner bark fibres of the paper mulberry tree, gathered and processed using time-honoured techniques.

The harvested lengthy fibres are formed into a dense web, resulting in durable, breathable and humidity-regulating paper, which has a distinctive texture and faint translucency.

Traditionally, the paper is written and painted on, as well as used for window treatments and as flooring.

Hanji now has broader uses, from applications in cultural heritage conservation to the making of furnishings, lighting design and lifestyle products.

These applications are demonstrated during the aptly named Hanji House exhibition during Maison&Objet 2026 – curated by The Korea Craft & Design Foundation (KCDF) – through the work of seven Korean companies specialising in Hanji.

"Hanji House is conceived as a showroom where visitors can experience Hanji's soft diffusion of light and responsiveness to airflow," said The Korea Craft & Design Foundation (KCDF).

"The exhibition presents Hanji not simply as paper, but as a contemporary material that can shape and define space."

Korean industrial design studio SWNA will present four furniture and lighting works exploring Hanji's adaptability, wherein the paper is combined with rigid materials, including metal and stone.

These works set out to demonstrate Hanji's potential in the contexts of contemporary furniture and spatial design, including a partition which doubles as lighting, and a cabinet and lighting pieces made up of graceful curves.

Alongside SWNA, Korean companies Hanji Park Materials Lab, Fides International Co., Toolpress, Somidang, Marquage G, Curated Columns and Pulbat will also present select works.

These range from traditional handmade Hanji and conservation paper to crafts, stationery, interior objects, fragrance products and lighting.

Hanji House takes place ahead of UNESCO's decision regarding whether to inscribe "traditional knowledge and skills associated with the production of Hanji and related cultural practices in the Republic of Korea" on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

This decision is expected to be reached later this year.

"Hanji embodies centuries of craftsmanship and traditional papermaking knowledge while offering the sustainability and versatility sought by today's design industry," said Kyungbae Kim, president of KCDF.

"In this meaningful year marking the 140th anniversary of Korea-France diplomatic relations and with UNESCO's decision approaching, we hope to share the beauty and contemporary potential of Hanji with the world and create greater opportunities for businesses rooted in Korean traditional culture to expand internationally."

The Korea Craft and Design Foundation (KCDF) is a public institution under the Republic of Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism (MCST).

It will be on show in the Signature gallery of Hall 7 in the Paris-Nord Villepinte exhibition centre as part of Maison&Objet 2026 from 10 to 14 September.

For more information, visit the Maison&Objet website.

item.content:encoded:
Multiple skyscrapers and smaller structures have been constructed since the terrorist attacks on 11 September 2001 devastated Lower Manhattan. Here, we take a look at the site 25 years on.

In 1973, the World Trade Center complex comprised seven skyscrapers, including One and Two World Trade Center, the tallest buildings in the world at the time. All were destroyed in the terrorist attacks.

A quarter-century later, the site is now home to mostly glass-clad structures by some of the world's most famous architects.

Because of complicated jurisdiction, the rebuilding process took years, and the consortium of developers and governmental parties finally settled on a master plan by Studio Libeskind.

"I think that the impact [of 9/11] was on the whole world," Daniel Libeskind told Dezeen in 2021. "Everything changed in architecture after that. People were no longer willing to do it as before."

Beyond the infrastructural damage, the attacks reshaped the landscape of Lower Manhattan, including creating a toxic environment in the air in the surrounding parts of the city, the extent of which was recently released by the city government.

The rebuilding process began in earnest shortly after and continues today. Most of the planned buildings, except for the on-hold 5 WTC, have been completed.

In addition to the buildings listed below, other parks and city facilities were constructed.

Read on for the major buildings on the World Trade Center site. 

7 World Trade, SOM, 2006

Because it was technically outside of the Port Authority jurisdiction that the rest of the complex falls under, 7 World Trade was able to be rebuilt almost immediately after cleanup from the attacks had officially concluded, in 2002.

Designed by iconic skyscraper architect David Childs, it is a quiet and functional building and at 745 feet tall (227 metres), it is dwarfed by the other skyscrapers on the site. The original 7 WTC building interrupted the grid, but the grid around it was considered with the overall masterplan, and today Greenwich Street passes through the complex.

The National 9/11 Memorial, by Michael Arad/Handel Architects and Peter Walker, 2011

Ten years after the attacks, a memorial was completed on the site by a relatively unknown architect, Michael Arad, who embedded with Handel Architects to complete the structure despite disagreements between the stakeholders.

Today, the site has two granite-lined pits on the footprints of the Twin Towers and groves of trees in a park designed by Walker. The names of the victims were engraved into a parapet surrounding the site.

An underground museum designed by Davis Brody Bond with a panelled entry structure by Snøhetta also sits in the park and was completed in 2o14.

Find out more about the National 9/11 Memorial ›

Fiterman Hall, Pei Cobb Freed and Partners, 2012

An academic building, Fiterman Hall was first built in the late 1950s and was heavily damaged by debris during the attacks.

After it was demolished in 2009, Pei Cobb Freed and Partners built a brick-clad building with a recessed entry to serve the student population.

Four World Trade, by Fumihiko Maki, 2013

Designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki, Four World Trade was the first of the skyscrapers under the Libeskind masterplan to be completed.

In line with 2010s skyscraper construction, it is covered in a glass curtain wall with an unusual single setback on one side where the upper portion slims and is trapezoidal. It rises 978 feet (298 metres).

One World Trade Center, by SOM, 2014

When it opened in 2014, One World Trade Center, once called Freedom Tower, was the tallest skyscraper in the Western Hemisphere and also the most expensive skyscraper ever built. Its height of 1776 feet (541 metres) was helped along by the massive antenna at its crown.

SOM's design replaced an initial design by Libeskind.

It has a faceted glass-covered facade and, because of security concerns, its base is clad in concrete and drapped in metal panels, which help integrate the base visually with the tower.

Find out more about One World Trade › 

World Trade Center Transportation Hub, by Santiago Calatrava, 2016

Serving as a connector for interstate transport, this transportation hub came to be called the Oculus and features massive steel ribs that cover the facade and extend outwards over the streets.

It features lofty internal spaces and skylights along the spine of the building that bring light into the spaces below, as most of the station is underground.

Find out more about The Oculus ›

Three World Trade, Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners, 2018

More than 15 years after the attacks, a 1,079-foot-tall (329 metres) skyscraper led by British architect Richard Rogers opened on the site.

Also mostly clad in glass, the building features steel bracing that run up the facade. The tower went up directly next to the Maki structure, making them appear as a pair, with similar dimensions on the glass window panelling.

Find out more about Three World Trade ›

St Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church, by Santiago Calatrava, 2022

Built to replace a church on the site this building is raised off the ground because of a security centre underneath.

It was informed by Byzantine architecture and features thin sheets of Pentelic marble that allow the structure to be illuminated from the inside at night.

Find out more about St Nicholas Greet Orthodox Church ›

Perelman Performing Arts Center, by Rex, 2023

Sited directly next to One World Trade, the Perelman Center sits on a plinth above the ground, in part because of the Port Authority infrastructure below. Architecture studio Rex had to deal with these constraints as well as the groundwork for a Frank Gehry building that was originally planned for the site.

Like St Nicholas,  the cubic structure is clad in thin marble that allows it to be illuminated. It has a series of modular theatre spaces inside.

Find out more about the Perelman Center ›

Two World Trade Center, by Foster + Partners, 2031 (planned)

Two World Trade Center could be the final piece in the decades-long development puzzle that is the World Trade Center site.

The glass-clad skyscraper will rise 1,226 feet (373 metres) and step up towards the crown. The design has been in contension with Foster + Parnters being replaced by BIG and then being reinstated. The studio released new renderings of the skyscraper before it broke ground in July 2026.

Find out more about Two World Trade Center ›

item.content:encoded:
An "angled, folded form" clad in charred cedar defines this holiday home, designed by Japanese studio Keiji Ashizawa Design to embrace the surrounding landscape while maintaining its inhabitants' privacy.

The studio designed the 225-square-metre holiday home for a family to use either alone or with guests.

Located on the Yatsugatake mountain plateau in central Japan, the house has an unusual shape that was designed to suit its surroundings.

"Although surrounded by abundant nature, the site sits within a residential area of holiday homes," studio founder Keiji Ashizawa told Dezeen.

"The house was carefully positioned and shaped to remain open to the surrounding landscape while avoiding direct views toward neighbouring properties," Ashizawa continued.

"The placement of the windows follows the same approach, framing nature while maintaining a sense of privacy."

The one-storey building has a gentle bend that creates angles that enclose its garden.

"In response to the surrounding views, the movement of natural light, and the scale of the house in relation to the landscape, an angled, folded form was developed to sit naturally within the site," Ashizawa said.

House in Yatsugatake was clad in yakisugi, a traditional Japanese charred cedar. The material was allowed to be used because the home is not in a densely populated area, where Japan has strict fire regulations.

"Unlike in central Tokyo, timber cladding is permitted in this area, allowing yakisugi to form an integral part of the exterior expression," Ashizawa said.

Ashizawa's studio also took the climate of the region into consideration when designing the house, which is located close to the road and also contains a garage.

"The house rests on a concrete foundation that becomes more exposed as the ground falls away across the sloping site," Ashizawa said.

Read:

Keiji Ashizawa creates holiday home within historic machiya

"Its relatively high profile also responds to the winter snowfall of Yatsugatake, following a construction approach commonly found in timber houses in colder regions," Ashizawa continued.

The holiday home has a central entrance, with a living, dining and kitchen area, loft and guest room in the western wing and private rooms and bathrooms to the east.

Keiji Ashizawa Design used oak wood for the interior, which features exposed sloping beams and windows close to the roof that frame the garden.

A skylight above the mezzanine loft lets light into the living room area.

To create a connection with the garden, the studio added full-width timber-framed windows in the bathroom that give panoramic views of the surrounding forest.

"By carefully reading the existing topography, trees, light, and wind, and allowing the architecture to respond quietly to them, we sought to create a home in which the surrounding landscape gradually reveals itself over time," the studio said.

Keiji Ashizawa Design has previously created an eight-room Tokyo hotel and a holiday home in a historic machiya.

The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku.
