item.content:encoded:
London may have a lot to shout about design-wise, but is it actually possible to survive as a creative in one of the world's most expensive cities? Ahead of London Design Festival, we spoke to five local designers about the challenges they face.

"I'm willing to live very modestly" said Tessa Silva

"Financially, I've had the toughest start to the year that I've had in the 10 years since graduating. I was teaching and assisting another artist before, I had my finger in a couple of other pies, but I let it all fall by the wayside. I suddenly found myself in a position where I didn't have anything to fall back on. It's taught me I have to keep connections with people and let them know I can still work for them, even if it seems like I have a big commission.

"Any time I do make money, I put it back into making new things in my studio. I'm willing to live very modestly, and hopefully that pays off one day. I don't buy new clothes or go out for dinner a lot; I make my own packed lunches. I live in a small flat that I've made beautiful – that's just part of choosing to live in London.

"A good currency for designers is doing swaps with people. I've gotten a photographer to photograph my work because I've given them a piece of my furniture, or I've got some nice jewellery because I've swapped it for work. It's a way of owning a few precious things when you can't afford to pay upfront for them.

"Even though this year has been really hard, I've been getting a few bites this summer that are making me excited and make me think this could be something long term and sustainable for the future, which is a really nice feeling."

Tessa Silva is exhibiting at Max Radford Gallery's Progressive Permanence

"You find nifty ways of transporting wood when you're going on a bike everywhere" said Jake Robertson

"Work for a designer who's got plenty of work for you to do, and they might be keen for you to use their workshop in your spare time – that's what James Shaw has done for me. I had to get inventive and learn how to make stuff that can fold up, disappear, and slip into the cracks of the workshop so I'm not taking up someone's space. It does mean you've got to graft outside of work and on the weekend, but it gave me access to great machinery.

"A great place to go for cheap offcut materials is Renée Materials. You'll find stuff there that you would never think could make furniture. I cycle – I'm not paying for transport, I can't do it – but you find nifty ways of transporting wood when you're going on a bike everywhere.

"I don't really make money from my practice. I've sold a couple of things, but it's not a money-making business. Hopefully one day I can get there, but that's a reason I would suggest people work part-time or full-time for a designer. I don't have to keep pumping my own work out. I also need a job that pays the rent. I can make good work and keep putting those things out – I don't need to dilute my Instagram by constantly putting stuff out for likes when that doesn't equal more sales."

Jake Robertson is exhibiting at Out of Worky and Design Everything's With Limitations

"My hack is trying to overcome my feeling of cringe" said Hanna Fastrich

"There are a lot of challenges in London, but it's a super-rich environment, and what's most important to me is my community. I have friends from uni or group exhibitions that are also designers, and we support each other. I work on ceramics and metal in my workshop, and sometimes I want to do some wood or something else, which a friend can give me access to. There's a beautiful sharing economy in my community – there's no gatekeeping.

"I always intensely apply to open calls, prizes and grants. I get loads of rejections, but every once in a while you get a yes. In the beginning, it felt cringe to reach out to people or send an email with my portfolio to a gallery, so my hack is trying to overcome my feeling of cringe and not to think about the worst possible outcome. Someone could say no and reject you, but that's not a horrible outcome, it's just a numbers game in the end."

Hanna Fastrich is exhibiting at Slancha's Hanging Baskets

"I turned to using waste materials as a necessity" said ThisIsByron

"My biggest overhead is material costs. That's how I turned to using waste materials – as a necessity. I then looked at what I could find within London and made a patchwork series with hardwood offcuts I found from various studios.

"I currently have a part-time job at the Royal Academy Schools as a workshop tutor. It's important I earn a wage that supports London living but also pays back into my studio.

"London is tricky, but it's also a bit of magic. Unit.d in Haggerston is like a church service affair where designers descend each month to hang out and share ideas – this only exists because of living in the city."

ThisIsByron is curating We Lift Each Other

"It's more valuable to have relationships with expert makers" said Marc Sweeney

"After I graduated in London, I moved back to Scotland and quickly discovered that I wasn't part of any design community. I may as well have been making work on the moon – there's just no point doing it if nobody's engaging with you.

"I am wrestling with the balance of being in London to network and work freelance, and I'm going to be teaching at Instituto Marangoni, then coming up to Scotland to make things. My family runs a passenger boat business on Loch Lomond, so we've got unbelievable workshop facilities. The long-term plan is to have a space in London, but it is eye-wateringly expensive – almost pretty much unaffordable for a single emerging designer.

"I'm a hands-on maker, but my work's got to a point where I need the help of experts. I'm outsourcing some work, or certain stages of my work. It's more valuable to have relationships with expert makers, which there are loads of in London, than it is to have your own space with machinery and you're trying to do absolutely everything yourself."

Marc Sweeney is exhibiting at Slancha's Hanging Baskets

Dezeen Showroom: the rugged aesthetic of the Australian outback meets the sophistication of contemporary design in the Cattle armchair, created by Gibson Karlo for the brand Design By Them.

Karlo took inspiration from the industrial metalwork seen on structures such as silos in the Australian rural landscape for the Cattle chair, adapting a style of joint where tubular metal is flattened and screwed together at points of intersection.

The usually rugged joint is given a refined and softened interpretation in the chair, combined with invisible connections and high-gloss finish in two refined shades: Merlot and Camel.

"The compressed tubular connection is a process rooted in agricultural metalwork," said Karlo. "We refined the typically harsh transition between round tube and flat surface, allowing the two forms to flow together and making the join a defining feature of the piece."

The Cattle chair's steel frame is paired with plush upholstered cushioning that drapes over the armrests and backrests.

The upholstery is available in a curated selection of fabrics from leading textile brands Kvadrat and Maharam.

In this episode, Dezeen features editor Nat Barker and design editor Jennifer Hahn are joined by editor Tom Ravenscroft to discuss the Dyson CameraJet.

The team have their take on the much-discussed launch, and come up with their own suggestions for future Dyson products.

Then, they consider a landmark new building in north London that is held up by a stone exoskeleton, in what has been billed a world-first.

item.content:encoded:
The Craft x Tech exhibition at the V&A will see artisans from Japan's Tokai region collaborate with international designers, including Philippe Malouin and Bethan Laura Wood, for London Design Festival.

The project aims to explore how traditional craft techniques can be used in new ways to create contemporary designs.

"We are not necessarily looking for the most famous crafts, but for techniques that seem to contain possibilities that have not yet been fully explored," Craft x Tech founder Hideki Yoshimoto, who worked on the project with curatorial director Maria Cristina Didero, told Dezeen.

"A craft may have developed over hundreds of years for a very particular purpose, but the knowledge accumulated within it can often have a much wider relevance than the objects it traditionally produces."

This year's edition of Craft x Tech, which first launched in 2024, focuses on craftsmanship from Japan's Tokai region.

It sees David Caon work with Yohei Ito, Lanzavecchia + Wai with Takanori Senda, Wood with Hiroyuki Murase, Malouin with Shigeyuki Ando, Eugene Kangawa with Mayuki Kato and Atang Tshikare with Tomoyuki Matsuda.

The aim was to not make the pairing of the designers and craftspeople "too obvious," Yoshimoto said.

"A certain distance between the designer and the craftsperson is useful: rather than simply applying a new design to an existing technique, they have to find their own point of connection, and that is often where something genuinely new begins," he explained.

For the designers, the collaboration provided an opportunity to work in new ways.

Industrial designer Caon, who created the Fushi modular ceramic console and lighting piece together with Ito of ceramic brand Fudogama, said he designed the original concept and this was then adapted by Ito.

"The original vision and the resulting piece are very different, but the spirit has been preserved by the understanding we both developed through our collaboration," Caon told Dezeen.

"Fushi is a piece created very much in my own language, but the distinct and beautiful green glaze and, indeed, the precision of the pieces is representative of Fudogama craftsmanship."

The resulting piece uses traditional oribe glaze to dramatic effect.

"The individual modules that make up the final assemblages are made to be identical," Caon said. "The oribe glaze, however, reacts completely unpredictably, removing any sense of uniformity across the surface of the piece."

Read:

Fourteen must-see exhibitions and installations at London Design Festival 2026

Also taking part in the exhibition is UK designer Wood, whose Kataginu light collection with artisan Murase of textile company Suzusan "celebrates the 'magic' of tying, binding and folding at the heart of the shibori dyeing technique," Wood told Dezeen.

Named for kataginu, a traditional Japanese sleeveless vest, the colourful lampshades have sculptural forms that also draw on rain chains, temple roofs and folded paper masks.

They were made using a dying technique called arimatsu narumi shibori, which also influenced the final design.

"The design process establishes a direct connection between three-dimensional folded construction, the resulting dyed pattern, and the final form of each light," Wood said.

"Central to the collection is an exploration of the unpredictable colour transitions that occur when two dyes interact, capturing the 'living' quality of the dye as it responds to folding, binding and manipulation."

Her work was partly informed by previous designs by Suzusan that had also used textiles.

"I wanted to expand on this and develop the textile and bespoke lighting component together to make a family of lighting that combined the final results of shibori alongside keeping elements of the folding, stitching and binding that are normally removed during the process," Wood said.

"I worked with Suzusan to choose colours that also reacted well when illuminated – I love that the soft gentle pastel pink transforms into an almost neon colour when lit."

French designer Malouin wanted his Kasane design, made with Ando of the Aichi Prefecture brand Ando Cloisonne, to be closely connected to the brand's language but reinterpreted through his own approach.

"I wanted the result to feel contemporary without being disconnected from what they traditionally produce," Malouin told Dezeen. "The final design is a series of functional boxes which, when stacked together, form a sculptural totem."

The restraints of the process also had an effect on the design process, with Malouin deciding to make smaller items than he had first wanted due to the size of the kiln.

The designer, who says his work is "rarely decorative" worked with Ando to find the right approach to the surface decoration of the vessels.

"I wrapped sheets of paper around full-scale models of the boxes and marked them freely and almost randomly with a large felt-tip pen," Malouin said.

This led to an unusual design with an "intuitive" feel that represented both Malouin's designs and Ando Cloisonne's craftsmanship.

"The final objects bring together the simplicity of my forms and mark-making with the extraordinary precision and care of Shigeyuki Ando’s cloisonné technique," Malouin said.

"There is something surprising about seeing such a spontaneous, handmade pattern translated through such a meticulous and highly skilled process. That contrast is where the design represents us both."

Also on show at LDF is a collection of reinterpreted Marcel Breuer furniture and many, many more must-see installations, as chosen by the Dezeen team.

The photography is by Masayuki Hayashi.
